Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization
for LLM Agent Training

Chenxu Zhang    Yaorui Shi    Wenlong Zhang    Jianchao Tan    Zihan Wang, Yiming Cheng
Abstract

Training long-horizon language model agents requires assigning credit to intermediate decisions from sparse terminal feedback. Within a finite group of sibling rollouts, useful action comparisons depend on their context, evidence for both alternatives, and how that evidence enters learning. We propose Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization (MCGPO), a procedure for constructing weighted action preferences from already collected trajectories. MCGPO defines comparison contexts with pre-action state summaries and observed rubric progress, annotated by task rules. Two-action support selects among ordered exact and coarse matching rules. Fixed folds separate candidate decisions from the terminal outcomes used to orient their preferences, and support-dependent evidence weights scale an auxiliary pairwise objective alongside shared GraphGPO task learning. MCGPO reuses rollout data and each response’s original history, preserving critic-free training. Across six environment–backbone settings with three training seeds each, MCGPO improves mean success over matched GraphGPO: by 0.47–1.46 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B, and by 3.96 and 5.16 points on WebShop with Qwen3-4B and 8B. The ALFWorld gains build on baseline success above 92%, where remaining headroom is limited. Integrated success improves in three of four Qwen2.5 settings. Three-seed factorial controls support opposite-fold evidence and evidence weighting; joint state–rubric matching achieves the highest mean in all four representation-control settings.

1 Introduction

Training large language model agents requires credit assignment: sparse terminal rewards must guide the intermediate actions that shape task outcomes (Zhou et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). In ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) and WebShop (Yao et al., 2022), success depends on a sequence of interdependent decisions. Group-relative reinforcement learning offers critic-free updates by comparing outcomes within a group of sampled responses or trajectories (Shao et al., 2024; Ahmadian et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025). For multi-turn agents, GiGPO localizes these comparisons at recurring anchor states (Feng et al., 2025), while trajectory-graph methods extract step credit from collected transitions (Li et al., 2026b; Cheng et al., 2026). However, grouping by repeated states or transitions can compare decisions with different prior task progress, obscuring what their outcome contrast represents.

This mismatch arises when the same state summary describes different remaining decision problems. A page, location, or inventory summary may omit progress established before the current choice. Consequently, an action taken after more prerequisites have been met can inherit a higher success rate, while a useful action taken earlier can receive weaker relative feedback. Their outcome contrast can mix prior progress with the contribution of the current action. A captured ALFWorld task illustrates this representational issue: two empty-handed visits to the same countertop share a coarse state key, although one follows acquiring and relocating a target object (Appendix D). Adding context can separate such decisions, but stricter conditions also reduce the repeated evidence available for comparing different actions.

Recent work enriches comparison context to address this tension. HGPO combines groups at multiple history depths, and BiPACE uses policy representations and action-conditioned peer baselines (He et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). Task structure offers another source of context: explicit criteria guide reward aggregation (Gunjal et al., 2025; Lv et al., 2026), policy stages and memory (Li et al., 2026a), and milestone-level credit (Wang et al., 2026d; Qian et al., 2026). However, an explicit preference between different actions also needs evidence for both alternatives. A richer context can leave one action poorly supported, so a larger outcome gap may reflect only a few trajectories. The remaining challenge is to select comparisons and weight their influence using the evidence available within a finite rollout group. This leads to our research question:

Research Question How can a finite group of existing rollouts supply supported local action preferences for policy learning?

We introduce MCGPO (Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization) to construct auxiliary action preferences from collected sibling rollouts. The core idea is to select a comparison context supported by both actions before forming a weighted preference. Match groups pre-action decisions by state summaries and observed rubric progress, with a rule-derived frontier annotating progress. It tries ordered exact and coarse state rules, selecting the first with evidence for both actions. Label uses terminal outcomes from the opposite fixed fold to orient pairs and assign support-discounted evidence weights. Learn optimizes a weighted pairwise objective alongside the shared GraphGPO task objective. The labels express observational outcome contrasts under the rollout policy; their weights control each pair’s optimization contribution. MCGPO reuses rollout data and preserves critic-free training and each response’s original history.

We evaluate MCGPO on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B, using three training runs per setting. Mean success improves over matched GraphGPO in all four settings by 0.47–1.46 percentage points, including ALFWorld baselines already above 92% success. A three-seed WebShop extension yields gains of 3.96 and 5.16 points with Qwen3-4B and 8B, respectively. Integrated success over the full training horizon improves in three Qwen2.5 settings, with positive paired differences in each of their three seeds. Three-seed factorial controls support opposite-fold evidence and evidence weighting. Across all four representation-control settings, joint state–rubric conditioning raises three-seed mean success over both State-only and Rubric-only matching. These results demonstrate performance gains across the tested backbones and support joint state–rubric conditioning as an effective comparison design.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    Supported local preference construction. We combine explicit comparison contexts, two-action support checks, and opposite-fold terminal evidence within an existing rollout group.

  • •

    Evidence-weighted policy learning. We connect these observational preferences to an auxiliary pairwise objective while retaining the shared task objective and original response histories.

  • •

    Evaluation of the construction and its scope. Matched comparisons, supervision controls, and representation diagnostics assess overall utility and setting-dependent component effects.

2 Related Work

Agent training and group-based credit.

Agent RL learns from interaction outcomes (Zhou et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025), with GRPO, RLOO, and DAPO estimating within-group advantages (Shao et al., 2024; Ahmadian et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025). GiGPO groups anchor states; HGPO combines historical-context depths (Feng et al., 2025; He et al., 2026). SALT matches recent interaction histories, while GraphGPO and RTMC aggregate credit through transition graphs and shared-state trees (Li et al., 2026b; Cheng et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). In the same sparse-reward, long-horizon setting, G2PO merges identical observations into a global state-transition graph and standardizes temporal-difference errors across edges to assign action credit (Wang et al., 2026c). AT-GRPO adapts tree-expansion depth to dialogue stage (Peng et al., 2026); STAPO selects steps using state-normalized entropy and combines trajectory-aware rewards with trajectory-independent penalties (Qi et al., 2026). Other designs use peer baselines, progress signals, or hierarchical updates (Wang et al., 2026a; Fan & Liu, 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2026; Jin et al., 2026). ECPO calibrates anchor-state credit using action-return shrinkage and reliability gates (Li et al., 2026c). MCGPO instead constructs action-pair supervision: pre-action state and rubric progress define comparability, two-action support selects the matching resolution, and opposite-fold outcomes label an auxiliary pairwise objective.

Task-structured supervision.

Task structure supports rubric rewards, exploration, and finite-state reward representations (Gunjal et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026; Toro Icarte et al., 2022). RubricEM organizes stages and memory; GEAR models criterion dependencies (Li et al., 2026a; Lv et al., 2026). SRaR, TRCA, and DRACO provide rubric-based step feedback (Xie et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Gandhi et al., 2026). BEACON combines milestone groups with reward shaping (Wang et al., 2026d); MileGPO infers milestones and traps from rollout graphs (Qian et al., 2026). MCGPO uses task-specific progress extractors to condition comparisons, with terminal outcomes supplying preference labels. SALT and MileGPO derive their comparison structure from histories and observed graphs.

Process, preference, and value supervision.

Process supervision extends terminal feedback (Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2024). DPO, REBEL, SimPO, and Contrastive Preference Learning optimize response or sequential-policy comparisons (Rafailov et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2024; Hejna et al., 2024); Step-DPO uses step preferences (Lai et al., 2024). Agent Q, VinePPO, OmegaPRM, and RTPO obtain intermediate evidence through search or additional continuations (Putta et al., 2024; Kazemnejad et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026d). POISE and SAPO learn value baselines or joint policy–value models (Choi et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026). MCGPO reuses collected sibling rollouts, separating candidate decisions from label contributors with fixed folds. Appendix Table 4 compares these designs.

3 Methodology

For each task xx, πold\pi_{\rm old} collects eight sibling trajectories τi\tau_{i} containing observations si,ts_{i,t}, responses zi,tz_{i,t}, canonical actions ai,ta_{i,t}, and terminal success yi∈{0,1}y_{i}\in\{0,1\}. Rollout slots define fixed folds ℐ0,ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1} of four trajectories each. MCGPO turns these rollouts into local preferences through Match–Label–Learn (Figure 2). In each direction, one fold supplies candidate decisions and the other supplies outcome evidence; swapping roles uses both halves.

3.1 Task-conditioned matching (Match)

A comparison context combines the pre-action state summary with observed task progress:

gi,t(ℓ)=(h(ℓ)​(si,t),Ci,t,Fi,t),ℓ∈{exact,coarse}.g_{i,t}^{(\ell)}=\big(h^{(\ell)}(s_{i,t}),C_{i,t},F_{i,t}\big),\qquad\ell\in\{\mathrm{exact},\mathrm{coarse}\}. (1)

Here Ci,tC_{i,t} contains rubric channels with finite positive pre-action status, and Fi,tF_{i,t} annotates inactive criteria enabled by task rules. Exact and coarse are ordered state-matching rules that preserve (C,F)(C,F); coarse abstracts identity fields and can include task-relevant bins. Appendix A.1 specifies the fields and extractors.

At each rule, each trajectory contributes its first eligible visit to a context. Candidate row pairs p=((i,t),(j,u))∈𝒞c(ℓ)p=((i,t),(j,u))\in\mathcal{C}_{c}^{(\ell)} come from distinct trajectories in fold cc, share a key gp(ℓ)g_{p}^{(\ell)}, and take distinct actions ap,bpa_{p},b_{p}. Let ℰ1−c(ℓ)​(g,a)\mathcal{E}_{1-c}^{(\ell)}(g,a) contain opposite-fold trajectories whose retained visit to gg takes action aa, and let na(ℓ)​(g)=|ℰ1−c(ℓ)​(g,a)|n_{a}^{(\ell)}(g)=|\mathcal{E}_{1-c}^{(\ell)}(g,a)|. The balanced support is n⋆(ℓ)​(p)=min⁡{nap(ℓ)​(gp(ℓ)),nbp(ℓ)​(gp(ℓ))}n_{\star}^{(\ell)}(p)=\min\{n_{a_{p}}^{(\ell)}(g_{p}^{(\ell)}),n_{b_{p}}^{(\ell)}(g_{p}^{(\ell)})\}, giving

ℓ⋆(p)=minexact≺coarse{ℓ:p∈𝒞c(ℓ),n⋆(ℓ)(p)≥m}.\ell^{\star}(p)=\min_{\mathrm{exact}\prec\mathrm{coarse}}\{\ell:p\in\mathcal{C}_{c}^{(\ell)},\ n_{\star}^{(\ell)}(p)\geq m\}. (2)

We use m=1m=1. Pairs without a supported rule are omitted. This gate precedes the outcome test: a supported exact match retains that rule even if its later contrast falls below threshold. Appendix A.1 gives the first-visit and eligibility definitions.

Let p^1−c(ℓ)​(g,a)\widehat{p}_{1-c}^{(\ell)}(g,a) be mean terminal success over ℰ1−c(ℓ)​(g,a)\mathcal{E}_{1-c}^{(\ell)}(g,a). At the selected key and resolution,

Algorithm 1 and the parameter settings appear in Appendix A.

3.3 Evidence-weighted policy learning (Learn)

Each preferred response should receive a larger policy improvement than its paired alternative. Using the original token histories Hi,t,kH_{i,t,k} and response mask mi,t,km_{i,t,k}, define the length-normalized log-probability change

dθ​(i,t)=∑kmi,t,k​[log⁡πθ​(zi,t,k∣Hi,t,k)−log⁡πold​(zi,t,k∣Hi,t,k)]max⁡(1,∑kmi,t,k).d_{\theta}(i,t)=\frac{\sum_{k}m_{i,t,k}[\log\pi_{\theta}(z_{i,t,k}\mid H_{i,t,k})-\log\pi_{\rm old}(z_{i,t,k}\mid H_{i,t,k})]}{\max(1,\sum_{k}m_{i,t,k})}. (5)

For pairs colocated in actor microbatch ℬ\mathcal{B}, the auxiliary loss is

ℒpair=∑(+,−)∈𝒫ℬc+,−​softplus⁡(−[dθ​(+)−dθ​(−)])max⁡(1,⌊|ℬ|/2⌋).\mathcal{L}_{\rm pair}=\frac{\sum_{(+,-)\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}}}c_{+,-}\operatorname{softplus}(-[d_{\theta}(+)-d_{\theta}(-)])}{\max(1,\lfloor|\mathcal{B}|/2\rfloor)}. (6)

Normalization by the microbatch’s pairing capacity makes the contribution scale with supervision supply; c+,−c_{+,-} controls each pair’s influence. The complete rollout group also supplies GraphGPO (Cheng et al., 2026) task advantages, giving

ℒactor​(ℬ)=ℒtask​(ℬ)+λpair​ℒpair.\mathcal{L}_{\rm actor}(\mathcal{B})=\mathcal{L}_{\rm task}(\mathcal{B})+\lambda_{\rm pair}\mathcal{L}_{\rm pair}. (7)

Here ℒtask\mathcal{L}_{\rm task} is the shared clipped policy loss with reference-policy and entropy terms (Appendix A.3). Tasks without preferences still receive this task update. The construction reuses sampled trajectories and policy log probabilities, preserving critic-free training. Appendix A.2 derives the local pairwise update.

4 Experiments

We organize the evaluation around four questions: whether MCGPO improves task completion and learning progress (RQ1), how comparison conditions, outcome evidence, and preference learning contribute (RQ2), how matched contexts produce weighted supervision on WebShop (RQ3), and whether the WebShop gains extend to Qwen3 backbones (RQ4).

4.1 Experimental Setup

4.1.1 Benchmarks and Models

We evaluate household interaction in ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) and product search and purchase in WebShop (Yao et al., 2022). The main experiments use Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024), with training seeds 0, 1, and 2. GraphGPO supplies the shared task-credit objective and matched baseline, measuring the effect of the complete rubric-conditioned preference branch. WebShop rubric extraction uses structured training information from the goal scorer, including attribute, option, and price matches and a pre-purchase preview score (Appendix A.1). Controls include GraphGPO with rubric-event shaping. For Qwen3-4B/8B, GraphGPO + shaping uses the same scorer information as MCGPO through training rewards, with three seeds per backbone.

4.1.2 Implementation Details

Within each backbone, MCGPO and GraphGPO use the same rollout, optimizer, and environment settings. Following the agent protocol of Feng et al. (2025), the Qwen2.5 policy conditions on the two most recent interaction steps and generates reasoning inside <think> tags followed by an action inside <action> tags. Each response is limited to 512 generated tokens. The environment horizons are 50 turns for ALFWorld and 15 for WebShop.

Each policy update uses 16 task groups with eight sibling rollouts per group. We train for 250 policy updates with rollout temperature 1.0, a constant learning rate of 10−610^{-6}, weight decay 0.01, and KL coefficient 0.01. The 1.5B and 7B runs use two and four GPUs, respectively, with tensor-parallel sizes of two and four. MCGPO uses the fixed preference-construction settings in Table 6. The Qwen3 extension uses action-only responses with thinking disabled. Resource settings, environment prompts, and an illustrative rollout appear in Appendices B, F, and G, respectively.

Evaluation.

Every five updates, we sample one rollout for each of the same 128 validation tasks at temperature 0.4. To reduce sensitivity to individual checkpoints and sampled evaluation rollouts, our primary metric is mean success over the last five scheduled evaluations (L5L_{5}). All matched runs use the same end-of-budget window. We first average within seed and then report the mean and sample SD across seeds. Appendix C provides precise definitions, seed-level results, and summaries of learning progress.

4.2 RQ1: Does MCGPO Improve Task Completion and Learning Progress?

Table 1 reports ALFWorld and WebShop results, including published references, task-category success, and graded scores. Appendix C (Table 10) provides paired uncertainty estimates and complementary readouts for the matched runs.

Task completion.

MCGPO improves mean success over matched GraphGPO in all four settings: by 1.04/1.46 percentage points on ALFWorld and 1.09/0.47 points on WebShop at 1.5B/7B. ALFWorld success rises from 92.60%/94.84% to 93.65%/96.30%, reducing the already-small remaining failure rate by approximately 14%/28%.

Where the gains appear.

ALFWorld’s largest category gains occur on Look (5.07/6.93 points at 1.5B/7B); Heat and Cool also improve at both sizes. On WebShop, success counts completed tasks, while the graded score also credits partial matches. At 1.5B, higher success accompanies a graded-score decrease from 88.79 to 86.83; at 7B, the scores are nearly equal.

Learning progress.

Figure 3 shows an earlier rise in success for the 1.5B models. At update 100, the smoothed advantage is 7.60 points on WebShop and 3.54 on ALFWorld. A retrospective summary of the complete, unsmoothed curves integrates success over updates 0–250 and divides by 250 (Table 10). The resulting gains are 1.25/1.46 points on ALFWorld and 2.98/−0.02-0.02 on WebShop at 1.5B/7B; the first three settings improve in each of their three seeds. This comparison measures learning progress along the policy-update axis. We also compare task success at matched interaction budgets below. Appendix C reports uncertainty across the three training seeds; Appendix C.5 gives all four curves.

Matched interaction budgets.

We complement the update-axis curves with a retrospective budget comparison on Qwen2.5-1.5B. For each training seed, we select the scheduled checkpoint pair with the largest shared training-transition budget among pairs whose relative budget difference is below 1%. Selection uses budgets alone. Figure 5 in Appendix C.2 reports raw checkpoint success: MCGPO raises the mean from 92.97% to 95.57% on ALFWorld and from 76.04% to 79.43% on WebShop, gains of 2.60 and 3.39 points. WebShop improves in all three paired seeds; ALFWorld’s differences vary across seeds. Appendix C.2 gives the selected checkpoints, counted interactions, and uncertainty.

4.3 RQ2: Which Parts of the Supervision Design Matter?

We test three design choices: task conditions for matching, the outcome evidence used to orient preferences, and the objective that transfers those preferences to the policy. Table 2(a) compares Full with four Qwen2.5-1.5B variants, using one training run per variant in each environment.

Comparison conditions and outcome evidence.

w/ Shuffled Rubric permutes pre-action (C,F)(C,F) labels among same-task decision rows, disrupting their alignment with actual progress. Success falls by 2.34 points on WebShop and 0.63 on ALFWorld. The Candidate-progress labels variant uses the candidate trajectories’ progress evidence in place of opposite-fold terminal outcomes to label comparisons, reducing success by 1.41 and 3.13 points. This joint replacement changes evidence source, label content, and available support. Its result favors the complete terminal-outcome preference design over the candidate-progress alternative.

How the supervision enters training.

w/o Pairwise Loss sets λpair=0\lambda_{\rm pair}=0 while retaining preference diagnostics; its success drops by 1.41 and 0.78 points. GraphGPO + Rubric Shaping adds positive-progress rewards and regression penalties to the task rewards, retaining GraphGPO credit assignment with the pairwise loss disabled. This event-shaping baseline scores 8.28 and 2.66 points below Full. It compares two uses of the rubric channels under the stated shaping rule and coefficient. The three-seed Qwen3-4B/WebShop factorial controls in Table 2(b) show gains of 2.34–2.40 points from opposite-fold evidence and 1.61–1.67 points from evidence weighting, with all four contrasts positive in every seed. Appendix C.3 reports configurations and paired intervals. The Qwen3 experiments additionally compare MCGPO with GraphGPO + shaping under the same scorer access (Appendix C.3).

Comparison representation.

Joint state–rubric conditioning gives the highest three-seed mean success in all four settings, exceeding State-only by 3.96–9.90 percentage points and Rubric-only by 5.15–9.01 points (Appendix C.4). The gains persist at the terminal evaluation in all four settings. With preference construction and the learning objective fixed, these gains support conditioning action comparisons and their terminal evidence jointly on state and progress. WebShop State-only already retains task-match score bins in its coarse state, placing this comparison within a scorer-assisted training setting.

4.4 RQ3: What Preferences and Weights Does the Construction Supply?

We examine preference construction on WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B, following supported comparisons through outcome-based labeling and evidence-weighted learning. Figure 4 covers all 750 updates from three runs: the matching resolution that supplies pairs, agreement with candidate outcomes, and the weight assigned to the evidence.

Matching supplies comparisons under sparse action support.

Of 1,990 accepted preferences, 1,805 (90.70%) use coarse matching, which relaxes state detail while retaining rubric progress and dependency coordinates. Average supply declines from 3.99 pairs per update in updates 26–50 to 2.08 in 226–250, with coarse matching dominant throughout. The weaker-supported action has one evidence trajectory in 1,547 pairs (77.74%); the remaining 443 have two for each action.

Outcome evidence determines direction and strength.

On WebShop, the preferred candidate succeeds while its alternative fails in 1,093 pairs; the reverse occurs in 124, and 773 have equal outcomes. This gives 74.35% pooled agreement when ties receive half credit. Every plotted window has a three-seed mean above 50%, showing a persistent association between preferences inferred from the evidence fold and outcomes in the separate candidate fold. The evidence fold’s mean absolute outcome contrast is 0.781; accounting for action support and matching resolution yields a mean evidence weight of 0.208 (Figure 4c). Agreement measures association with candidate terminal outcomes, which also reflect subsequent actions.

Connection to policy learning.

The auxiliary loss is active in all 511 updates with accepted preferences (68.13% of training updates). RQ2 complements these supervision diagnostics with loss-removal, shuffled-rubric, and representation controls of policy performance.

4.5 RQ4: Do the WebShop Gains Extend to Qwen3 Backbones?

We extend the matched GraphGPO–MCGPO comparison to Qwen3-4B and 8B on WebShop with seeds 0, 1, and 2. These runs share the training budget and evaluation schedule and use action-only responses with thinking disabled.

MCGPO raises mean success from 78.18% to 82.14% at 4B and from 79.69% to 84.84% at 8B, gains of 3.96 and 5.16 percentage points, respectively. All six paired runs improve, with gains of 2.66–5.78 points at 4B and 2.50–9.22 points at 8B (Table 9). This consistency across seeds extends the evidence to both Qwen3 model sizes under action-only responses. A scorer-matched reward-shaping comparison appears in Appendix C.3.

5 Conclusion

MCGPO constructs action preferences by matching state and rubric progress within existing rollout groups. Opposite-fold terminal outcomes supply preference directions, and an evidence-weighted pairwise loss complements the GraphGPO task objective.

Across six environment–backbone settings, MCGPO improves three-seed mean success over matched GraphGPO, including ALFWorld baselines above 92% and Qwen3 WebShop gains of 3.96 and 5.16 points. Representation and factorial controls support joint context matching, opposite-fold evidence, and evidence weighting; scorer-matched comparisons favor MCGPO over reward shaping. Together, these results support extracting useful action-level supervision from existing rollout groups.

Appendix A Algorithm and comparison construction

This section specifies the comparison sets, evidence weights, and actor objective used in Section 3. Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete update. The same eight sibling trajectories supply the task objective and the auxiliary preferences.

Table 4 compares the task and preference interfaces with the related designs discussed in the main text.

A.1 Comparison keys and first visits

Each decision has a pre-action state summary hh, active rubric criteria CC, and rule annotation FF. Boolean true and finite positive channel values activate membership in CC; extractor diagnostics are excluded. Appendix D.1 gives the environment-specific channels. For vocabulary VV, prerequisites P⁡(j)P(j), blocking sources B⁡(j)B(j), and the set VblockV_{\rm block} of blocking-source nodes,

F(C;V,Gx)={j∈V∖(C∪Vblock):P(j)⊆C,B(j)∩C=∅}.F(C;V,G_{x})=\{j\in V\setminus(C\cup V_{\rm block}):P(j)\subseteq C,\ B(j)\cap C=\emptyset\}. (8)

FF annotates inactive criteria whose prerequisites are satisfied and which are not blocked. The opening status is empty; later records use the extractor schema. In ALFWorld, this vocabulary change can affect the first evidence row retained at the opening boundary.

Rollout slots define ℐ0={0,2,4,6}\mathcal{I}_{0}=\{0,2,4,6\} and ℐ1={1,3,5,7}\mathcal{I}_{1}=\{1,3,5,7\}. For key gg, each trajectory contributes its first eligible visit:

ti(ℓ)​(g,b)\displaystyle t_{i}^{(\ell)}(g;b) =min⁡{t≥b:gi,t(ℓ)=g},\displaystyle=\min\{t\geq b:g_{i,t}^{(\ell)}=g\}, (9)
𝒢c(ℓ)​(g,b)\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{c}^{(\ell)}(g;b) ={(i,ti(ℓ)(g;b)):i∈ℐc,ti(ℓ)(g;b)<∞}.\displaystyle=\{(i,t_{i}^{(\ell)}(g;b)):i\in\mathcal{I}_{c},\ t_{i}^{(\ell)}(g;b)<\infty\}.

Candidate groups use b=1b=1, while evidence groups use b=0b=0. Candidates have different canonical actions. Opposite-fold first visits provide the support counts and empirical action-success rates used by the support gate in Eq. 2. The constructor retains the earliest qualified comparison per trajectory pair, then allocates up to two disjoint decision-row pairs per task and direction.

The four-trajectory evidence fold permits balanced action support n⋆∈{1,2}n_{\star}\in\{1,2\}. Its smallest nonzero binary-outcome contrast is 1/31/3, so the configured threshold retains every non-tied supported contrast. Shrinkage contributes 1/31/3 or 1/21/2 at the two support levels. Invalid groups keep their task update with zero auxiliary weight.

A.2 Outcome provenance and pairwise update

Let DD fix the admitted batch, rollout slots, keys, actions, turn indices, and hyperparameters. In candidate direction cc,

𝒫c​(D,yc,y1−c)=Φc​(D,y1−c).\mathcal{P}_{c}(D;y_{c},y_{1-c})=\Phi_{c}(D,y_{1-c}). (10)

Thus changing ycy_{c} leaves that direction’s labels and weights unchanged under these fixed inputs. The reverse direction uses ycy_{c} as evidence. Batch admission uses whole-group outcomes and lies outside this conditional property. Finite-support contrasts remain observational estimates; the evidence weight controls their optimization contribution.

Local pairwise gradient.

During an actor update, pair membership, orientation, the rollout policy, and weight cpc_{p} are fixed. With δθ=dθ​(+)−dθ​(−)\delta_{\theta}=d_{\theta}(+)-d_{\theta}(-) and gθ±=∇θdθ​(±)g_{\theta}^{\pm}=\nabla_{\theta}d_{\theta}(\pm), one pair contributes

∇θℓp=−cp​σ​(−δθ)​(gθ+−gθ−).\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{p}=-c_{p}\,\sigma(-\delta_{\theta})(g_{\theta}^{+}-g_{\theta}^{-}). (11)

The actor colocates both rows in a microbatch, applies the normalization in Eq. 6, and adds the scaled auxiliary term to the task loss. RQ2 measures the policy effect of this addition.

A.3 Shared task objective

The GraphGPO task branch uses Ri,tgraph=10​γD⁡(si,t+1)R_{i,t}^{\rm graph}=10\gamma^{D(s_{i,t+1})}, where DD is directed distance to an observed successful goal; unreachable states receive one more than the largest finite distance. Let Zi,t=∑kri,t,ktokZ_{i,t}=\sum_{k}r^{\rm tok}_{i,t,k} be the token-level task score, including invalid-action penalties. The advantage sums the normalized graph return within the task’s anchor state group and the normalized task score within its response group:

A^i,ttask=Norm𝒰x,si,t⁡(Ri,tgraph)+Norm𝒰x⁡(Zi,t).\widehat{A}_{i,t}^{\rm task}=\operatorname{Norm}_{\mathcal{U}_{x,s_{i,t}}}(R_{i,t}^{\rm graph})+\operatorname{Norm}_{\mathcal{U}_{x}}(Z_{i,t}). (12)

Normalization uses the group mean and sample SD with 10−610^{-6} in the denominator. Singleton step groups have centered score zero; singleton task groups use mean zero and unit scale. Both task-credit coefficients are one, and each row advantage is broadcast to its valid response tokens.

For token ratio ρ=πθ/πold\rho=\pi_{\theta}/\pi_{\rm old}, define ℓclip=max⁡{−ρ​A,−clip⁡(ρ,0.8,1.2)​A}\ell_{\rm clip}=\max\{-\rho A,-\operatorname{clip}(\rho,0.8,1.2)A\} and ℓdc=min⁡{ℓclip,−3​A}\ell_{\rm dc}=\min\{\ell_{\rm clip},-3A\} when A<0A<0, with ℓdc=ℓclip\ell_{\rm dc}=\ell_{\rm clip} otherwise. The masked token mean ⟨⋅⟩ℬ,m\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal{B},m} gives

ℒtask=⟨ℓdc​(ρ,A^task)+0.01​K^−0.001​ℋ​(πθ)⟩ℬ,m,\mathcal{L}_{\rm task}=\left\langle\ell_{\rm dc}(\rho,\widehat{A}^{\rm task})+0.01\,\widehat{K}-0.001\,\mathcal{H}(\pi_{\theta})\right\rangle_{\mathcal{B},m}, (13)

where K^=clip⁡(ev−v−1,−10,10)\widehat{K}=\operatorname{clip}(e^{v}-v-1,-10,10) and v=log⁡πref−log⁡πθv=\log\pi_{\rm ref}-\log\pi_{\theta} on sampled tokens. The mask follows the response format in Appendix F. Gradient accumulation and distributed reduction use the shared actor configuration.

Appendix B Experimental setup

This section records the shared training recipe used by GraphGPO and MCGPO. The environment prompts appear in Appendix F. Comparisons within a backbone use the same task data, response protocol, optimizer, and evaluation grid.

B.1 Training and evaluation configuration

Table 7 summarizes the environment and backbone profiles. Each update uses P×GP\!\times\!G admitted trajectories; shared dynamic group filtering can require additional generated groups when enabled.

Every setting trains for 250 policy updates with eight sibling rollouts per task, response length at most 512 tokens, rollout temperature 1.0, learning rate 10−610^{-6} with a constant schedule, and weight decay 0.01. Gradient checkpointing is enabled. The task objective’s clipping and regularization coefficients are specified in Appendix A.3. Validation samples one rollout on each of the same 128 tasks every five updates at temperature 0.4.

Continuation and evaluation lineage.

Main runs retain their archived →→2500\!\to\!150\!\to\!250 protocol. Mechanism controls target 250 updates from initialization and use their corresponding Full reference seed (WebShop seed 0; ALFWorld seed 1). The ALFWorld controls use the corrected epoch-loop budget. Recovery restores model, optimizer, scheduler, random-number state, dataloader state, and the update counter. Reported scheduled evaluations follow the retained checkpoint lineage; reload evaluations and rolled-back branches are excluded. Controls are separate executions, so their recorded recovery histories can differ.

Appendix C Supplementary policy results and ablations

These results complement RQ1, RQ2, and RQ4 with seed-level readouts, uncertainty, and the control definitions. Success is reported in percent; paired gains use percentage points.

C.1 Readouts and seed-level results

Our primary metric summarizes late-training success over the final five scheduled evaluations of the shared 250-update budget. Averaging these evaluations reduces sensitivity to an individual checkpoint and its sampled rollouts. For each training seed, we compute

L5=15​∑t∈{230,235,240,245,250}S⁡(t).L_{5}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{t\in\{230,235,240,245,250\}}S(t). (14)

Here S⁡(t)S(t) is validation success at update tt. The same budget and end-of-budget window apply to all matched methods and seeds. We average within each seed before computing the mean and sample SD across seeds. Table 8 retains all designated Qwen2.5 seeds; Table 9 provides the three-seed WebShop extension underlying Table 3.

Learning progress and uncertainty.

Per-seed endpoint values E250=S⁡(250)E_{250}=S(250) are retained in Table 8 for completeness. Normalized integrated success summarizes learning progress over the complete raw evaluation grid tj=5​jt_{j}=5j:

Is=1250​∑j=150Ss​(tj−1)+Ss​(tj)2​(tj−tj−1).I_{s}=\frac{1}{250}\sum_{j=1}^{50}\frac{S_{s}(t_{j-1})+S_{s}(t_{j})}{2}(t_{j}-t_{j-1}). (15)

Table 10 reports success and integrated success with paired intervals Δ¯±4.30265​sΔ/3\overline{\Delta}\pm 4.30265\,s_{\Delta}/\sqrt{3}. The three training seeds determine uncertainty; evaluations along one training trajectory are dependent. The L5L_{5} and integrated-success intervals span zero in all four Qwen2.5 settings. These intervals quantify the uncertainty accompanying the observed mean gains.

C.2 Matched training-transition budgets at 1.5B

This retrospective diagnostic covers the twelve Qwen2.5-1.5B runs: MCGPO and GraphGPO on ALFWorld and WebShop, each with training seeds 0, 1, and 2. The effective configurations disable dynamic rollout filtering and collect 16×8=12816\times 8=128 trajectories per update. The logged mean episode length L¯m,s,u\overline{L}_{m,s,u} counts active environment steps per unique trajectory. Actor padding duplicates rows, while this metric deduplicates them by trajectory identity. We reconstruct cumulative training transitions as

Bm,s​(t)=∑u=1tround⁡(128​L¯m,s,u).B_{m,s}(t)=\sum_{u=1}^{t}\operatorname{round}\!\left(128\,\overline{L}_{m,s,u}\right). (16)

With 128 trajectories, the three-decimal logged mean uniquely determines the integer total; every reconstructed update passes the rounding check. We follow the retained checkpoint lineage across resumes. Validation, reload-only evaluation, rolled-back updates, and unfinished failed attempts are outside this training budget.

For each environment and seed, we enumerate the scheduled checkpoint pairs tM,tG∈{5,10,…,250}t_{M},t_{G}\in\{5,10,\ldots,250\} satisfying

|BM,s​(tM)−BG,s​(tG)|min⁡{BM,s​(tM),BG,s​(tG)}<0.01,\frac{|B_{M,s}(t_{M})-B_{G,s}(t_{G})|}{\min\{B_{M,s}(t_{M}),B_{G,s}(t_{G})\}}<0.01, (17)

where MM and GG denote MCGPO and GraphGPO. We maximize the smaller of the two budgets, breaking ties by smaller relative mismatch and then larger combined update count. Selection uses the interaction counts alone. The plotted readout is raw validation success at the selected checkpoint, aggregated equally over the three training seeds. The budget labels average the paired costs across seeds. These checkpoint readouts are distinct from the primary L5L_{5} metric.

Mean gains are 2.60 points on ALFWorld and 3.39 on WebShop. WebShop has three positive paired differences; ALFWorld has one positive, one zero, and one negative difference. Descriptive paired 95% Student-tt intervals (df=2\mathrm{df}=2) are [−13.90,19.11][-13.90,19.11] and [−1.50,8.27][-1.50,8.27] points for ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively.

C.3 Mechanism controls

Table 2(a) reports one completed Qwen2.5-1.5B run per variant and environment. The candidate-progress control uses candidate trajectories’ progress in place of opposite-fold terminal outcomes, jointly changing evidence source, labels, support, and weights. The loss-removal control sets λpair=0\lambda_{\rm pair}=0 while retaining construction diagnostics. These single-run comparisons evaluate the specified interventions; replication would estimate their variability.

The rubric-shaping control keeps GraphGPO credit and adds

Δ​rt=0.05​Ntincrease−0.05​Ntdecrease\Delta r_{t}=0.05\,N_{t}^{\rm increase}-0.05\,N_{t}^{\rm decrease} (18)

to the executed response’s last valid token before advantage computation, with pairwise learning disabled. Counts include changes in graded and count-valued channels; a channel can increase more than once. This Qwen2.5 comparison evaluates the event-shaping rule at a fixed coefficient.

Factorial controls of evidence source and weighting.

Table 2(b) crosses two factors on Qwen3-4B/WebShop: opposite-fold versus same-fold terminal evidence, and evidence-based versus uniform loss weights. All four variants share initialization, training data, action-only prompts with thinking disabled, and 250 updates with 16 task groups of eight trajectories per update. We use seeds 0, 1, and 2, learning rate 10−610^{-6}, and fixed folds {0,2,4,6}\{0,2,4,6\} and {1,3,5,7}\{1,3,5,7\}. The construction parameters in Table 6 and λpair=0.05\lambda_{\rm pair}=0.05 are shared, without variant-specific tuning.

A (Full) and C use the four opposite-fold trajectories as terminal evidence; B and D use the four same-fold trajectories, including the candidates themselves. A and B retain the original evidence-weight formula. C and D assign equal loss weights to the selected preferences while preserving their original total weight. Matching rules, support thresholds, and pair-selection criteria otherwise remain fixed.

Table 12 reports individual seeds and paired contrasts. Opposite-fold evidence improves success under both evidence weighting (A−BA-B: +2.34 pp) and uniform weighting (C−DC-D: +2.40 pp). Evidence weighting improves success with both opposite-fold (A−CA-C: +1.61 pp) and same-fold evidence (B−DB-D: +1.67 pp). All four contrasts are positive in every seed, and their paired 95% intervals lie above zero. These results support each design choice under both settings of the other factor.

Scorer-matched Qwen3 comparison.

This experiment compares two ways of using the same scorer-derived supervision, testing whether the complete MCGPO preference-learning scheme improves on reward shaping. For Qwen3-4B/8B, GraphGPO + shaping uses all scorer information available to MCGPO (Appendix A.1) through training rewards. Table 13 reports the three-method comparison and paired gains across seeds 0, 1, and 2. MCGPO improves mean success over shaping by 2.29 points at 4B and 2.66 at 8B, with positive gains in all six paired runs. These results support the complete MCGPO scheme as a more effective use of the scorer signals than the compared reward-shaping alternative.

For differences dsd_{s}, the paired 95% Student-tt interval is d¯±t0.975,2​sd/3\bar{d}\pm t_{0.975,2}\,s_{d}/\sqrt{3}, where sds_{d} is their sample SD. It summarizes training-seed variability under the paired-tt approximation; both intervals lie above zero.

C.4 Representation controls

State-only, Rubric-only, and Full use the state coordinate, rubric coordinates, and their joint context, respectively, with the same preference construction and actor objective. Table 14 reports seeds 0, 1, and 2 in all four settings. Full has the highest mean under both readouts throughout, exceeding State-only by 3.96–9.90 and Rubric-only by 5.15–9.01 percentage points on the primary readout. Full and State-only produce different selected preference sets during training. Joint keys retain revisits after progress changes and condition candidate actions and opposite-fold evidence on both state and progress. State-only can merge different progress stages; Rubric-only can merge different environmental situations. The gains support joint context for selecting the auxiliary learning signal. WebShop State-only already includes task-match score bins, so this control compares how structured training information is used. Appendix D illustrates visit retention and support in a separate diagnostic sample.

C.5 Learning curves and supervision dynamics

This subsection supplies the full curves referenced by RQ1 and the aggregation definitions for RQ3. Figures 6 and 7 describe policy learning and interaction length over the same retained training runs.

Training behavior.

The ALFWorld analysis includes all 750 updates from three completed Full runs. Windows 26–50, 101–125, and 226–250 contain 25 updates per seed. Mean training success rises from 60.3% to 89.9% and 95.3%, while mean rollout length falls from 29.34 to 13.91 and 10.17 steps. Length counts active interactions per distinct trajectory, including successful, failed, and truncated runs under the 50-step cap. Mean anchor-state group size rises from 4.10 to 5.54 and 6.62; it counts decision rows sharing task and observation, including repeated visits. These are joint training trends; component effects are assessed in RQ2.

Preference supply and agreement.

Figure 4 uses all 750 WebShop 1.5B updates in nonoverlapping 25-update windows. Each seed contributes equally to the plotted means and sample SD. Counts include zero-pair updates; outcome ratios pool W,T,LW,T,L within each seed/window before aggregation. The pooled 74.35% agreement instead weights all 1,990 accepted pairs. Coarse matching supplies 1,805 pairs (90.70%).

Weights and entry into learning.

Evidence contrast and weight means first weight updates by accepted-pair count within each seed/window. Their pooled means are 0.781 and 0.208.

Among all pairs, 1,547 have balanced evidence support one and 443 have support two. The weight combines outcome contrast, support shrinkage, and matching resolution. TensorBoard values matched to the retained process and update confirm nonzero pairwise loss in all 511 updates with accepted pairs; all 239 empty-pair updates have zero loss. This establishes objective activation, complementing the loss-removal control in RQ2. All these counts describe the constructor’s selected output. Source logs retain the exact count identities and checkpoint lineage.

Appendix D Rubric, matching, and preference diagnostics

This section specifies the comparison keys used in RQ2 and supplies diagnostics for RQ3. The rubric specification defines recorded task progress; archived examples illustrate visit retention and matching support, and WebShop outcome diagnostics characterize selected preferences.

D.1 Environment rubric rules

Extractors run after each transition. The next decision uses that transition’s status as its pre-action CC and FF, following the opening convention in Appendix A.1. ALFWorld reads task metadata and tracks target-object sets 𝒜,𝒫,ℒ\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{L} for acquisition, processing, and placement. The required count is r=2r=2 for Pick2 and r=1r=1 otherwise. Successful take, process, and placement feedback updates these sets; entity matching preserves object-instance numbers.

WebShop reads browser-session fields and its existing goal scorer. Product-match channels therefore use additional structured training supervision, including scorer evaluation before purchase. Reusing rollouts saves trajectory collection while retaining this information requirement. The extractor’s task contract omits the target product identifier; the environment scorer retains its goal metadata. The adapters use deterministic rules and the benchmark scorer. With matched/requested attribute and option counts Ma,Mo,Na,NoM_{a},M_{o},N_{a},N_{o}, type score uu, and price predicate pp, purchase readiness is

qpreview=u​Ma+Mo+pNa+No+1.q_{\rm preview}=u\,\frac{M_{a}+M_{o}+p}{N_{a}+N_{o}+1}. (19)

Absent components and caught scoring errors retain initialized zeros. This includes an omitted option component for a no-option goal. Terminal evidence uses y=1[score≥0.999]y=\mathrm{1}[\mathrm{score}\geq 0.999].

Table 17 lists the task-rule graphs. All non-blocking edges supply the prerequisite tests in Eq. 8; the text-environment graphs have no blocking edges. ALFWorld’s coarse budget bin partitions the remaining horizon at 1/4,1/2,3/41/4,1/2,3/4. WebShop’s score bins use roundeven⁡(4​clip⁡(v,0,1))\operatorname{round}_{\rm even}(4\,\operatorname{clip}(v,0,1)). Action keys preserve canonical ALFWorld commands; WebShop uses navigation/purchase markers and goal-aware search, product, and option keys from the pre-action page, with goal-token overlap thresholds 0.15,0.35,0.600.15,0.35,0.60. Missing required trace fields disable auxiliary supervision while retaining the task update. Progress-measurement errors can change groups and action support; extractor precision and recall against independent annotations remain unmeasured.

D.2 Matching support and a captured example

The census uses ten archived update-60 captures: 160 task instances and 1,280 trajectories across the four text settings. These captures are a separate diagnostic sample from the training runs in Table 14. Each candidate fold contains four trajectories; groups count first eligible visits per trajectory and key. Coverage divides records in groups of size at least two by all retained records at that resolution. Figure 8 reports the distribution over groups; Table 18 reports coverage over records and counts supported pairs. Both precede outcome filtering.

Exact and coarse are evaluated separately, so supported-pair counts can overlap. On these archived snapshots, Full replay reproduces the stored pairs and directions; State-only selects the same pairs, with no accepted pairs in the WebShop subset after outcome filtering. These statistics characterize local matching availability. Figure 9 illustrates how progress preserves a revisit as a distinct comparison context; Table 14 assesses the benefit of applying joint context throughout training.

D.3 WebShop agreement with candidate outcomes

Table 19 pools WebShop W/T/LW/T/L counts of 1404/1261/188. Agreement measures association with candidate terminal outcomes after preference construction; RQ2 supplies the policy controls. These archived samples contain repeated training observations; the complete 250-update WebShop 1.5B diagnostics and objective-activation check appear in Appendix C.5.

Appendix E Limitations

MCGPO is evaluated on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen backbones. Transfer to other domains requires suitable state summaries, rubric channels, and task rules; WebShop also uses structured goal-scorer information during training. Preferences are inferred from finite groups of observational rollouts: coarse matching can retain outcome-relevant differences, and terminal success depends on subsequent decisions as well as the matched action. Evidence weighting moderates the influence of sparse comparisons, while direct validation of local action preferences remains an important direction. Our main comparisons use three training seeds and repeated evaluation on a fixed validation set, so small gains retain statistical uncertainty. Evaluation with broader model families, more seeds, and independent test tasks would further assess generalization and statistical precision.

Appendix F Environment Prompts

GraphGPO and MCGPO use the same environment templates within each backbone setting. Each filled template forms a user message in the backbone’s chat template; rubric coordinates are computed by the training adapters. The boxes below give the interaction prompts, including their response instructions. Only line wrapping, trailing whitespace, and the typographic hyphen in e-commerce are normalized.

Placeholders in braces are filled from the current environment state. The first decision omits the history block; later decisions include up to the two most recent observation–action pairs, as specified in Table 7. Each history entry has the form [Observation n: ’observation’, Action n: ’action’]. step_count counts completed actions and current_step=step_count+1. A recorded ALFWorld example appears in Appendix G.
